title: Heel Pain and Plantar Fasciitis: Causes, Relief and When to See a Specialist
metaDescription: Sharp heel pain with the first steps in the morning? Understand plantar fasciitis causes, proven home treatment, and when to consult a foot & ankle surgeon in Thane.
intro: Sharp, stabbing heel pain with your first steps in the morning is the hallmark of plantar fasciitis — inflammation of the thick band of tissue supporting the arch of your foot. It is one of the most common reasons patients visit a foot and ankle clinic.

sections.heading: Why it happens
bullets: Prolonged standing or walking on hard surfaces
Flat feet or very high arches
Tight calf muscles and sudden increases in activity
Unsupportive footwear and excess body weight

sections.heading: What actually works
sections.body: More than 9 in 10 people improve within about 10 months with simple measures, according to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons — but only with consistent treatment over weeks, not days.
bullets: Daily plantar fascia and calf stretching
Silicone heel cups or custom arch-support insoles
Night splints for stubborn morning pain

sections.heading: When to see a specialist
sections.body: If heel pain persists beyond 6–8 weeks of home care, a foot and ankle specialist can confirm the diagnosis, rule out stress fractures or nerve entrapment, and discuss options such as shockwave therapy or a steroid injection, used for pain relief. Surgery is considered only if there is no improvement after about 12 months of good non-surgical care.

faqs.q: Is a heel spur the cause of my pain?
faqs.a: Usually not. Heel spurs are seen on X-rays of many pain-free people. The pain comes from the inflamed plantar fascia, which is why treatment targets the fascia rather than the spur.

faqs.q: How long does plantar fasciitis take to heal?
faqs.a: Many people start to feel better within a few weeks to a couple of months of consistent stretching and footwear changes, but full recovery can take longer. More than 9 in 10 improve within about 10 months with simple measures.

faqs.q: Do I need an MRI for heel pain?
faqs.a: Rarely. Diagnosis is clinical in most cases. Imaging is reserved for atypical pain or when symptoms fail to improve with proper treatment.
